19963-stop-look-and-dig:
George O. Smith wrote Stop, Look, and Dig, a science fiction story of hidden talents. Its narrator runs his perception up a whole city block. He takes cover behind telephone poles and front steps as he goes. By the block's end he knows it as if he had made it himself. Perception, in the story, is a sense that can be aimed and extended. Smith built many tales on such engineered abilities.

Smith was an electronics engineer who wrote for Astounding magazine. His fiction loves gadgets, signals, and competent men. A perceiving hero turns detection into a superpower of attention. The story's title twists the railroad crossing warning cleverly. Stop, look, and dig: caution becomes method. It is pulp science fiction with an engineer's soul.
20893-a-guide-to-methods-and-observation:
Historical novels like Les Miserables can teach, says Calvin Olin Davis in his guide to history teaching. Dramas, poems, essays, and reviews all earn a place in his scheme. The book, from 1914, bears the full title Studies in High School Observation in part.

Davis trains history teachers to watch classes and weigh what truly works. Methods, sources, and aims fill chapters built from real school visits. His work served the new science of teaching as schools grew vast. Readers in education can see classroom study in its earnest youth, keen to make history live for pupils, not just fill their heads.
21360-old-gold-the-cruise-of-the-jason-b:
Two wealthy Englishmen resolve to sail as far up a great South American river as anyone ever has. George Manville Fenn's tale has them choose the Amazon at last. They find the brig Jason and her skipper. Then they gain an unwelcome extra: Briscoe, a pushy young man who talks his way aboard with his stores and a servant.

It is very hot to start, in Guiana's damp, sticky heat where the muddy river looks oily. Attacks by local archers, a boat sucked toward a great cataract and saved by an eddy, and a trackway hauled past the falls follow. Above the falls they find a rock-hewn city in the cliffs, empty for centuries.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-abbey-of-gott: The Encyclopedia on Göttweig, the proud house above the Wachau and the Danube. Its Baroque halls gleam over the vineyards. Michael Ott gives its full history. Austria's monks at their grandest. Emperors hunted in its forests and slept in its guest rooms.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-adam-franz-le: A 1913 entry on Adam Franz Lennig — the Mainz churchman of the nineteenth century. Francis Mershman notes his reforms. He rebuilt Catholic life in his diocese. A pastor of the restoration age. His seminary trained a generation of priests. Mainz remembers its restorer.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-brunswick-bra: A 1913 entry on Brunswick — the Guelph duchy's church story. Benedict Guldner tells its storied past. Its princes led the Reformation's van. The old faith lingers in its enclaves. A land of the divided confession. Its Dankwarderode castle is famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-johann-bollig: A 1913 entry on Bollig — the Jesuit orientalist. Benedict Guldner honors his Arabic labors. His pen served the Roman schools. The order prized its learned son. The nineteenth century knew his name. His 1895 death is famed. His 1895 Arabic is famed. His 1895 Roman Arabic is famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-joseph-konig: A 1913 entry on König — a German writer of note. Patrick MacAuley surveys his works. Little survives about his life. The nineteenth century was his time. The learned press knew his pen. His 1890 works are famed. His 1890 writings are famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-leipzig: A 1913 entry on Leipzig — the Saxon diocese. Joseph Lins gives its founding story. Its bishops guard the trade-town flock. The entry keeps its modest record. A see of the German east. Its 1921 founding is famed. Its bishops are famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-schleswig: Schleswig became the diocese of the Danish borderland. This entry covers its bishops, its churches, and its history. The faith of the Jutland march: its old churches serve the duchy in the north of Germany's march in the borderland of the Danes.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-hedwig: St. Hedwig was the duchess of Silesia. This long entry examines her Trebnitz, her charities, and her cult. The mother of the Polish church: her new convent crowned Trebnitz in the 1200s' Silesia in the north of the duchy in the Oder.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-tewdrig: Tewdrig was the saint of Gwent. This entry traces his kingship, his battle, and his fame. The king of the Welsh border: his holy martyrdom crowned Gwent in the 500s' Wye in the river of the truly very old border.

doe-osti-3365079-a-review-of-polymeric-n: Tiny particles built from polymers — long chain-like molecules — are becoming delivery trucks for medicine. doe-osti-3375119-kent-island-boundary-la: Kent Island got boundary-layer-campaigned, and this DOE report covers the field. The pages detail the campaign findings. The climate folks get their data. The report was field campaign. The data were climate. The Island were Kent. The layer were boundary.

gao-gaoreports-gao-05-423sphig: A panel of road-and-rail experts met under GAO's banner in 2005, and this highlights edition distills the debate over highway and transit dollars. Benefits, costs, and the hard choices between them get the compact treatment. The experts had spoken.
govdocs-archive_org-the-paulician-heresy:
Nina G. Garsoian studied the Paulicians, a medieval Armenian Christian sect, in The Paulician Heresy. Her work traces the group's origin and development as a dualist movement on the eastern edge of the Byzantine world.

The Paulicians rejected much of the church's structure, its priests, and its sacraments, and the empire hunted them for it over several centuries. Garsoian works from Armenian and Greek sources to separate the sect's real teaching from its enemies' charges, which were often wild. Her study became a landmark of heresy research. The full text serves students of medieval religion who need the evidence handled with care.
hunting-the-grisly-and-other-sketches-an: Theodore Roosevelt's Hunting the Grisly: big game of the West. The hunter-naturalist's sketches. Adventure and observation. A sportsman's classic, roosevelt hunts the Western grizzly, the hunter-naturalist, a sportsman's classic, Theodore Roosevelt, big game.
jack-rustig: Jack Rustig, Frederick Marryat's tale. The sailor's story. This book preserves that novel. Such papers rarely see the light of day. The file is now open to the public. Its contents inform the historical record.
lewie-or-the-bended-twig:
Sarah H. Bradford published Lewie, or The Bended Twig, in 1854. Alden, Beardsley issued it at Auburn and Rochester, New York. A motto verse praises a mother's gentle, mighty hand.

A mother alone may train and guide her plants, the verse says. Rightly trained, they blossom sweet; neglected, they wither. Contents open with Little Agnes, then Brook Farm and Christmas time. The bended twig image promises a tale of childhood shaping. Bradford's story follows how early training bends a life. The twig proverb was a favorite of Victorian moral tales. Bradford applies it to one child's whole upbringing.
lives-of-the-english-poets-from-johnson-:
Henry Francis Cary designed these lives as Johnson's continuation. His series runs from Johnson's own era toward Kirke White. Cary also wrote The Early French Poets, published in 1846. His Pindar odes in English verse reached a second edition.

The volume extends Samuel Johnson's famous Lives of the English Poets. Later poets whom Johnson never treated receive biographies here. Cary writes as translator, clergyman, and practiced man of letters. Readers get a nineteenth-century bridge from Johnson toward the Romantics. A memoir and literary journal of Cary were preparing then. His son's generation would publish the translator's own letters later.
plays-of-sophocles-oedipus-the-king-oedi:
Sophocles' three Theban plays appear here as the Oedipus Trilogy: Oedipus the King, Oedipus at Colonus, and Antigone. The English version is by F. Storr, once a scholar of Trinity College, Cambridge. It comes from the Loeb Library edition, first published in 1912.

An argument before the first play tells the old tale in brief. An oracle warned Laius that his son would kill him and wed his mother, Jocasta. The grown Oedipus kills Laius without knowing him, solves the riddle of the Sphinx, and takes the throne and the queen. When plague strikes Thebes, his search for the killer leads to himself.
t-mann-der-tod-in-venedig:
An aging writer on holiday in Venice becomes obsessed with a beautiful Polish boy and stays as cholera closes over the city. Mann's Der Tod in Venedig, given here in German, is his most famous novella. Gustav von Aschenbach, disciplined master of prose, watches his lifelong self-command dissolve in the Venetian heat.

Art, desire, and decay interlock in a design of terrible perfection. Every sentence of the original German carries the music translators struggle to keep. Aschenbach's fall is stately, sordid, and pitiable at once, which is the novella's cold power. Few short books have been argued over so much for so long. It remains the essential doorway into Mann for readers worldwide.
